chief_complaint: sudden drooping of left side of face, unable to close left eye, and drooling since waking up
hpi_details: Presents to urgent care in acute panic after waking up this morning to find the entire left side of his face completely paralyzed and drooping. Unable to close his left eye completely, causing irritation and tearing, and noticed tea dribbling out of the left corner of his mouth at breakfast. When attempting to smile, only the right side of his face moves. Also notes that everyday sounds seem painfully loud in his left ear (hyperacusis) and food tastes metallic/bland on the front of his tongue. Experienced a mild aching pain behind his left ear for two days before the facial weakness appeared. Denies arm or leg weakness, speech difficulty, double vision, or difficulty swallowing.
ideas: thinks he has suffered a massive stroke during the night and is permanently paralyzed
concerns: terrified he will never regain his facial appearance or ability to blink and speak normally
expectations: wants urgent brain CT scan to confirm stroke and immediate treatment to reverse paralysis
pmh: hypertension controlled on monotherapy, no prior neurological issues
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks socially on weekends, high school history teacher

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Bell's Palsy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Reassure patient regarding high spontaneous recovery rate (>80% complete recovery within 3-6 months) and clearly explain that this is NOT a brain stroke, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden drooping of left side of face, unable to close left eye, and drooling since waking up

Key HPI features: Presents to urgent care in acute panic after waking up this morning to find the entire left side of his face completely paralyzed and drooping. Unable to close his left eye completely, causing irritation and tearing, and noticed tea dribbling out of the left corner of his mouth at breakfast. When attempting to smile, only the right side of his face moves. Also notes that everyday sounds seem painfully loud in his left ear (hyperacusis) and food tastes metallic/bland on the front of his tongue. Experienced a mild aching pain behind his left ear for two days before the facial weakness appeared. Denies arm or leg weakness, speech difficulty, double vision, or difficulty swallowing.

Objective/Exam findings: Perform cranial nerve examination: ask patient to raise eyebrows/wrinkle forehead (CRITICAL DISTINCTION: complete absence of forehead wrinkling on the left confirms a Lower Motor Neuron lesion of cranial nerve VII; preservation of forehead wrinkling indicates an Upper Motor Neuron lesion/stroke due to bilateral cortical innervation of the forehead). Ask patient to squeeze eyes shut tightly (left eye fails to close - Bell's phenomenon visible where globe rolls upward), show teeth/smile (mouth deviates to the healthy right side), puff out cheeks (air leaks from left mouth corner). Test taste on anterior two-thirds of tongue and check hearing sensitivity. Inspect external ear canal and tympanic membrane: look for vesicular rash in concha/ear canal (to exclude Ramsay Hunt Syndrome / Herpes Zoster Oticus). Check all other cranial nerves and limb power (completely normal).
Relevant background/PMH: hypertension controlled on monotherapy, no prior neurological issues
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Bell's Palsy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute ischemic stroke (spares forehead, has limb signs) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any arm or leg weakness accompanying the facial droop — would suggest a stroke instead of Bell's palsy.
management_principles: After assessing for features of stroke or another secondary cause, explain that the presentation is most consistent with Bell's palsy and that recovery is common.

Initiate oral prednisolone: 50mg-60mg daily for 10 days (or 5-day high dose followed by tapering schedule), ideal if started within 72 hours of symptom onset to reduce nerve oedema and improve functional outcome
Consider adding antiviral (valacyclovir 1g TDS for 7 days) if severe complete paralysis or herpes zoster suspected
Protect the affected eye with lubricating drops by day, ointment at night, and eyelid taping during sleep when closure is incomplete.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 45M presents with acute unilateral facial paralysis affecting upper AND lower face (forehead, eye closure, mouth), accompanied by hyperacusis, loss of taste, and post-auricular pain. No limb weakness or dysphasia.
reference_soap.objective: Perform cranial nerve examination: ask patient to raise eyebrows/wrinkle forehead (CRITICAL DISTINCTION: complete absence of forehead wrinkling on the left confirms a Lower Motor Neuron lesion of cranial nerve VII; preservation of forehead wrinkling indicates an Upper Motor Neuron lesion/stroke due to bilateral cortical innervation of the forehead). Ask patient to squeeze eyes shut tightly (left eye fails to close - Bell's phenomenon visible where globe rolls upward), show teeth/smile (mouth deviates to the healthy right side), puff out cheeks (air leaks from left mouth corner). Test taste on anterior two-thirds of tongue and check hearing sensitivity. Inspect external ear canal and tympanic membrane: look for vesicular rash in concha/ear canal (to exclude Ramsay Hunt Syndrome / Herpes Zoster Oticus). Check all other cranial nerves and limb power (completely normal).
reference_soap.assessment: Bell's Palsy (Idiopathic Lower Motor Neuron Facial Nerve Palsy). DDx: acute ischaemic stroke / stroke in evolution (ruled out by forehead involvement and isolated VIIth nerve pattern without limb signs), Ramsay Hunt syndrome (check for ear vesicles/severe pain), Lyme disease (check tick exposure/erythema migrans), parotid gland tumour compressing VIIth nerve.
reference_soap.plan: Reassure patient regarding high spontaneous recovery rate (>80% complete recovery within 3-6 months) and clearly explain that this is NOT a brain stroke. Initiate oral prednisolone: 50mg-60mg daily for 10 days (or 5-day high dose followed by tapering schedule), ideal if started within 72 hours of symptom onset to reduce nerve oedema and improve functional outcome. Consider adding antiviral (valacyclovir 1g TDS for 7 days) if severe complete paralysis or herpes zoster suspected. Mandatory eye protection protocol: artificial tears/lubricating eye drops hourly during the day, thick lubricating eye ointment at night, and taping the left eyelid shut securely with surgical tape during sleep to prevent exposure keratopathy and permanent corneal ulceration.

learning_objectives: Differentiate Lower Motor Neuron facial palsy (forehead paralyzed, Bell's palsy) from Upper Motor Neuron facial weakness (forehead spared, stroke)
Systematically inspect the external ear canal for vesicular rash to rule out Ramsay Hunt Syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus)
Prescribe early high-dose oral corticosteroid therapy (prednisolone within 72 hours) to maximize facial nerve functional recovery
Formulate a strict, mandatory eye protection protocol (lubricants and nighttime eyelid taping) to prevent exposure keratopathy

teaching.one_liner: An idiopathic paralysis of the facial nerve causing sudden one-sided facial drooping, including the forehead — the forehead involvement is the key clue that distinguishes it from a stroke, which typically spares it.
differentials: Acute ischemic stroke (spares forehead, has limb signs)
red_flags: Any arm or leg weakness accompanying the facial droop — would suggest a stroke instead of Bell's palsy

must_ask.say: Can you wrinkle your forehead on that side, or is it completely still?
Did this come on suddenly, like overnight?
Any pain behind your ear, or does sound seem painfully loud?
Does food taste different on the front of your tongue?
Any weakness in your arm or leg, or trouble speaking?
